dm: Even the parts are reduced to atoms, And those atoms are divided into directional facets. Since the directional facets are also devoid of parts, They are like space; therefore, even atoms do not exist.
gm: And the part also by its division into particles, And that particle also by its division into directional parts, And since the division of directions is devoid of parts, It is like space; therefore, even particles do not exist.

dm: Such being the case, what discerning person Would be attached to forms that are like a dream? When the body is thus non-existent, Then who is a man and who is a woman?
gm: Thus, what intelligent person would be attached To form, which is like a dream? When the body does not exist in that way, Then what is a man and what is a woman?

dm: If suffering exists in its own right, Why does it not afflict those who are joyful? If happiness is real, why do those tormented by grief and the like Not find joy in delicious food and such?
gm: If suffering truly existed, Why does it not harm the very joyful? If happiness [truly existed], for those overcome with grief and so forth, Why do delicious foods and so forth not cause joy?

dm: If it is argued that it is not experienced because it is overwhelmed by something more powerful, How can that which is not of the nature of experience Be a sensation?
gm: If it is because it is overshadowed by something stronger That it is not experienced, How can that which is not of the nature of experience Be a feeling?

dm: If you say that suffering exists in a subtle state And its gross form has merely been removed, Then that is simply a state of joy other than that; If you say it is subtle, then that too is of the same nature.
gm: "Suffering exists in a subtle state; Has its gross state not been removed?" If you say, "That is merely a joy distinct from that," Then that subtle state too is [a state] of that [joy].

dm: If, because an opposing condition has arisen, Suffering is not produced, Then is it not established that what is considered "feeling" Is merely a stubborn conceptual attachment?
gm: If, because a contrary condition has arisen, Suffering does not arise, Is it not established that the conception of feeling Is merely conceptual clinging?

dm: For that very reason, one should meditate On this analytical investigation as its antidote; The meditative concentration arising from the field of such analysis Is the food of the yogi.
gm: For this very reason, the antidote to this Is to meditate on this analytical discernment; That which arises from the field of analysis Is the food of the yogi's concentration.

dm: If there is a gap between the sense faculty and the object, Where would those two meet? If there is no gap, they are but one; What, then, could meet with what?
gm: If there is a gap between the sense faculties and objects, Where would they meet? Even if there is no gap, they are a single entity, So what would meet with what?

dm: An atom cannot enter another atom, For it has no space and they are equal in size. Without entering, there is no mingling, And without mingling, there is no contact.
gm: An atom does not enter an atom, For they have no empty space and are of equal size. Without entering, there is no mixing, And without mixing, there is no meeting.

dm: How could it be logical to speak of "contact" Between things that have no parts? If you have ever seen contact occurring without parts, Then please demonstrate it.
gm: How could it be reasonable to say That what is partless can meet? If meeting and being partless Have been seen together, show it!

dm: For a consciousness that is formless, Contact is not at all logical. A collection also lacks substantial reality, Just as was previously analyzed.
gm: For consciousness, which has no body, Meeting is not reasonable at all. Neither is it for an aggregation, because it does not exist as a real entity, Just as was analytically examined before.

dm: If, in this way, there is no contact, From what could feeling arise? For what purpose is all this toil? What could cause harm to what?
gm: Thus, if contact does not exist, From what would feeling arise? What is the purpose of this weariness? What would harm what?

dm: When there is no experiencer at all, And feeling itself does not exist, Then, having seen this situation, Why does craving not turn away?
gm: When there is no feeler at all, And feeling also does not exist, At that time, having seen this situation, Why would craving not be turned away?

dm: Since seeing and even touching Are of the nature of dreams and illusions, And arise simultaneously with the mind, That feeling is not seen by it.
gm: Seeing or even touching, Have a nature like a dream or an illusion. Because it arises simultaneously with the mind, Feeling is not perceived by it.

dm: Even if born previously or later, They would be remembered but not experienced. The self does not experience itself, Nor is it experienced by others.
gm: Even by what arises before or after, It is remembered, but not experienced. It does not experience itself, And it is not experienced by others either.

dm: There is no experiencer at all, And therefore, feeling itself does not exist. Thus, how can this collection, Which is devoid of a self, be harmed by this?
gm: There is no feeler at all, Therefore, feeling itself is not real. Thus, for this selfless aggregate, How could it be harmed by this?

dm: The mind does not abide in the sense faculties, Nor in forms and so forth, nor in between them. It is not the mind within, nor is it without, Nor is it to be found anywhere else.
gm: The mind does not abide in the sense faculties, Nor in forms and so forth, nor in between them. The mind is not inside, nor is it outside, And it is not found anywhere else.

dm: That which is not the body, nor something other than it, Neither mixed with it nor separate in any way, Is not even the slightest thing; therefore, Sentient beings are by nature in the state of nirvana.
gm: That which is not in the body, nor anywhere else, Not mixed, nor apart from it anywhere, Is nothing whatsoever; therefore, Sentient beings are by nature in nirvāṇa.

dm: If consciousness existed prior to the object of knowledge, Then directed toward what would it arise? If consciousness and the object of knowledge are simultaneous, Then directed toward what would it arise?
gm: If consciousness exists before the object of knowledge, Directed towards what would it arise? If consciousness and the object of knowledge are simultaneous, Directed towards what would it arise?

dm: If, however, it exists after the object of knowledge, Then from what would consciousness arise? In this way, the arising of all phenomena Cannot be understood.
gm: Or if it exists after the object of knowledge, Then from what does consciousness arise? In this way, of all phenomena, Arising cannot be realized.

dm: If in that way the conventional does not exist, How could there be the two truths? Furthermore, if that conventional exists through another, How could sentient beings pass into nirvana?
gm: If, in this way, conventional reality does not exist, How could the two truths exist in that? And if that is due to another conventional reality, How could sentient beings pass into nirvāṇa?

dm: This is the conceptualization of another's mind; It is not one's own conventional reality. If that is later ascertained, then it exists; Otherwise, the conventional simply does not exist.
gm: This is the conception of another mind; It is not one's own conventional reality. If it is ascertained later, it exists; If not, conventional reality itself does not exist.

dm: Conceptual thought and the object to be analyzed Are both mutually dependent. Based upon what is renowned in the world, All analytical investigations are expressed.
gm: Conception and the object to be conceived, The two are mutually dependent. Relying on what is conventionally known, All analyses are expressed.

dm: When one analyzes with an analysis That is itself being analyzed, Then because that analysis is also to be analyzed, There is no end to it.
gm: When analysis Is analyzed by analysis, Then that analysis too, Because it is analyzed, has no end.

dm: When the object of analysis is thoroughly analyzed, There is no basis remaining for the analysis. Because there is no basis, it does not arise, And that is described as nirvana.
gm: If the object of analysis has been analyzed, There is no basis for analysis. Because there is no basis, it does not arise, And that too is expressed as nirvāṇa.

dm: For those who hold that these two are real, Their position is extremely difficult to maintain. If the object is established through the power of consciousness, What basis is there for the existence of consciousness itself?
gm: According to those who hold these two to be true, That very position rests in great difficulty. If the object is established by the power of consciousness, What is the basis for the existence of consciousness itself?

dm: If, however, consciousness is established through the object of knowledge, What basis is there for the existence of the object of knowledge? If they exist through mutual dependence, Then both of them will be non-existent.
gm: Or if consciousness is established from the object of knowledge, What is the basis for the existence of the object of knowledge? If they exist by the power of one another, Both also would not exist.

dm: If there is no father without a son, From what could the son himself have arisen? Without a son, there is no father; Likewise, both of them are non-existent.
gm: If without a son there is no father, From what does the son himself arise? In the absence of a son, there is no father; Likewise, those two themselves do not exist.

dm: Just as a sprout is produced from a seed, And the seed itself is known by that very sprout, Why is the existence of the object of knowledge not realized By the consciousness that arises from it?
gm: A sprout arises from a seed, and Just as that very seed is known by it, By consciousness, which arises from the object of knowledge, Why is the existence of that [object] not known?

dm: If a consciousness other than the sprout Realizes that the seed exists, Then by what means is the existence of that consciousness, Which realizes that object of knowledge, itself realized?
gm: By a consciousness that is other than the sprout, If the existence of the seed is known, By which that object of knowledge is known, From what is the existence of the consciousness itself known?

dm: For the time being, through worldly direct perception, All causes are seen. The distinctions in the lotus stalk and so forth Are produced by the distinctions among their causes.
gm: For now, by worldly direct perception, All causes are seen. The variations such as the stalk of the lotus Are produced by the variations of causes.

dm: If you ask what created the variety of causes, It is from the very variety of preceding causes. Why is a cause able to produce an effect? It is from the very power of the preceding cause.
gm: If one asks, what made the variations of causes? From the variations of prior causes themselves. Why are causes able to produce effects? From the power of prior causes themselves.

dm: If Īśvara is the cause of the world, Then for a start, explain who Īśvara is. If you say he is the elements, that may be so; But why weary yourself over a mere name?
gm: If Īśvara is the cause of beings, Tell me, for now, what is Īśvara? If one says it is the elements, so be it; But what is the use of exhausting oneself over a mere name?

dm: However, because earth and the others are multiple, Impermanent, inert, and not divine, And because they are things to be trodden upon and are impure, They are not Īśvara himself.
gm: However, earth and so forth are multiple, Impermanent, devoid of movement, not divine, Objects to be stepped upon, and impure; They are not Īśvara himself.

dm: Īśvara is not space, because space is inert; He is not the self, as that has already been refuted. And if the creator is also inconceivable, What is the point of speaking of him as "inconceivable"?
gm: Īśvara is not space, because it is devoid of movement; He is not the self, because it was already refuted before; And as for a creator who is inconceivable, What is the use of speaking of the inconceivable?

dm: Furthermore, what is it that he is asserted to produce? Are not the self, the earth, and so forth, And the nature of Īśvara himself, also eternal? Since consciousness arises from objects of knowledge,
gm: And what is it that he wishes to produce? Are not the self, those such as earth, And the essence of Īśvara permanent? Consciousness arises from the object of knowledge, and

dm: Pleasure and pain have arisen from karma since beginningless time. Tell me, what is it that is created by him? If there is no beginning to the cause, How could there be a beginning to the effect?
gm: Happiness and suffering are from beginningless karma; Tell me, what was produced by him? If the cause has no beginning, How can the effect have a beginning?

dm: Why does he not create constantly? For he is not dependent on anything else. If there is nothing that was not created by him, Upon what would he depend?
gm: Why does he not create continuously? He does not depend on another. If there is nothing else that was not made by him, Upon what would he depend?

dm: If he depends on something, then the collection of conditions Is the cause, and not Īśvara. When the collection is present, he has no power not to produce, And without it, he has no power to produce.
gm: If he depends, then the collection itself Would be the cause, and not Īśvara. When assembled, there is no power not to produce, And without them, there is no power to produce.

dm: If he acts without desiring to do so, It follows that he is under the power of another. If he does desire to act, he is dependent upon that desire; If he is thus dependent, how can he be Īśvara?
gm: If Īśvara creates without desiring it, It follows that he is under the control of another. Even if he desires, he is dependent upon desire. If he creates, how is he Īśvara?

dm: Those who claim that atoms are eternal Have already been refuted previously. The Sāṃkhyas assert that a permanent Primal Substance Is the cause of the world.
gm: As for those who assert permanent atoms, They have also already been refuted earlier. The permanent Pradhāna is the cause of beings; This is what the Sāṃkhyas assert.

dm: The equilibrium of the qualities known as Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas Is proclaimed to be the Primal Substance; Their disequilibrium is said to be the world.
gm: The qualities known as Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas, Abiding in equilibrium, Are termed Pradhāna; In disequilibrium, they are said to be beings.

dm: It is illogical for a single entity to have three natures; Therefore, it does not exist. Likewise, the qualities themselves do not exist, Because they too each have a threefold nature.
gm: For one thing to have three natures Is illogical, therefore it does not exist. Likewise, the qualities do not exist, Because they too would each have three aspects.
